You’ve got this! 😊 - Midterm 2 grading is in progress. ## Recap: iClicker {.slide-your-turn .smaller} **Select all of the following statements which are TRUE.** - (A) Bag-of-words represents a document using word counts and preserves the order of its words. - (B) TF–IDF gives more weight to a term that is frequent in a document but rare across the collection. - (C) Dense retrieval can find relevant text even when the query and document use different words for the same idea. - (D) Supplying retrieved passages in a RAG prompt updates the generator's learned weights. - (E) A RAG system can generate an unsupported answer even when it retrieves relevant evidence. ::: {.notes} Correct answers: B, C, E. A: False. Bag-of-words discards word order, so it can miss differences in meaning caused by order. B: TF captures frequency within a document; IDF downweights terms that occur in many documents. C: Dense representations can capture semantic similarity beyond exact word overlap, though retrieval can still fail. D: False. Ordinary RAG changes the input context, not the generator's weights. E: Retrieval and generation can fail separately. Even useful passages do not guarantee that the generated answer follows the evidence. ::: ## Recap: Which model would you use? {.slide-your-turn .smaller} | Scenario | Model/Method | |-------------------------------------------------------|-------| | You have user–item ratings (e.g., movie ratings) and want to predict missing ratings. | ? | | You have a collection of documents without any labels and want to group them into themes. | ? | | You want to find catalog descriptions relevant to a customer’s question, even when they use different words for the same idea. | ? | | You have a small dataset with ~500 images containing pictures and names of 20 different Computer Science faculty members from UBC. Your goal is to develop a reasonably accurate multi-class classification model for this task.| ? | ::: {.notes} For the catalog scenario: dense retrieval using text embeddings and cosine similarity. Embed the question and catalog descriptions, then rank descriptions by similarity. This task asks for relevant source text; generating an answer would be an additional step. ::: ## Today's big questions {.slide-goals} 1. What changes when our data has a **time order**? 2. How can we **evaluate forecasts** without using future information? 3. How can we turn **past observations and time patterns** into useful features? 4. How can we forecast **multiple steps into the future**? Time order $\to$ evaluation $\to$ temporal features $\to$ forecasting ::: {.notes} Use bike rentals as the running example: what can we know at prediction time, how should we test our predictions, and what features help us predict future demand? Temporal features include calendar information, lagged observations, seasonality, and trends. Connect the feature choices to the strengths and limitations of linear and tree-based models. ::: ## Loan default prediction {.smaller} Each row describes a customer applying for a loan. **What type of model would you use to predict default?** | Customer | Income ($k) | Credit used (%) | Late payments | Employment | Default | |----------|------------:|----------------:|--------------:|------------|--------:| | 1 | 95 | 22 | 0 | Salaried | 0 | | 2 | 45 | 78 | 3 | Contract | 1 | | 3 | 120 | 30 | 1 | Salaried | 0 | | 4 | 60 | 65 | 2 | Self-employed | 1 | **Target:** default (1 = yes, 0 = no). Customer ID identifies the row. For this example, we treat customers as independent: **reordering rows does not change the prediction task.** ## Predict demand for bike rentals Suppose you want to predict the bike rental demand for the next three-hour period at a station in New York City. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ![](img/citibike.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} What features might help us make an accurate prediction? ::: :::: ## Citi Bike data {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {#ab8cf98f .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` starttime 2015-08-01 00:00:00 3 2015-08-01 03:00:00 0 2015-08-01 06:00:00 9 2015-08-01 09:00:00 41 2015-08-01 12:00:00 39 2015-08-01 15:00:00 27 Freq: 3h, Name: one, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} - Recorded every **three hours**; each timestamp marks the start of a period. - **Target:** rental count during that period. - Initially, our only input is **datetime**. - Nearby rental counts may be related: **time order matters**. ::: :::: **Using only the tools in your current toolbox, what model would you choose, and what challenges might you run into?** ## What do we know when we predict? {.smaller} At **09:00**, predict rentals during **09:00–12:00**. | Past observations | Prediction time | Target period | |:------------------|:---------------:|:--------------| | 03:00–06:00 and 06:00–09:00 counts are known | **09:00** | **09:00–12:00** count is unknown | - Each timestamp labels the **start** of a three-hour rental period. - Calendar features for the target period are known in advance. - Lag features use counts from **completed periods**. **Every feature must be available when we make the prediction.** ## Models for time series Two broad approaches: - Use **sequence models** that explicitly model temporal relationships, such as Transformers. - Use **tabular models with engineered temporal features**, such as Ridge, random forests, and gradient boosted trees. **Today: give familiar tabular models useful information about time.** ## Citi Bike data visualization ::: {#d0c6bb02 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Start date: 2015-08-01 00:00:00, End date: 2015-08-31 21:00:00 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-19-time-series_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-2.png){width=809 height=436} ::: ::: Do you see any daily patterns? Weekly patterns? Noise? ## ⛔️ Incorrect data splitting ::: {#c44a0726 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} train_df, test_df = train_test_split(citibike, test_size=0.2, random_state=123) print('Train largest date: ', train_df.index.max()) print('Test smallest date: ', test_df.index.min()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Train largest date: 2015-08-31 21:00:00 Test smallest date: 2015-08-01 12:00:00 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#88b8995b .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-19-time-series_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=790 height=330} ::: ::: ⛔️ We should never train on the future to predict the past! ## ✅ Correct data splitting Use the first **23 days for development** and hold out the last **eight days for one final test**. Choose features and models using temporal validation within the development period. ::: {#2ce7aed5 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} n_train = 184 train = train_df = rentals.iloc[:n_train] test = test_df = rentals.iloc[n_train:] ``` ::: ::: {#a387cee6 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-19-time-series_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=790 height=330} ::: ::: ## Cross-validation with time series {.smaller} - Each validation window comes **after** its training window. - Use three expanding folds within the **first 23 days**; each validation window covers **four days**. ```text Time → Training grows; validation moves forward Fold 1 [Train: 11 days][Valid: 4 days] Fold 2 [Train: 15 days][Valid: 4 days] Fold 3 [Train: 19 days][Valid: 4 days] ``` ::: {#53f92113 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=3, test_size=32) for fold, (fit_rows, valid_rows) in enumerate(cv.split(train), start=1): print(f"Fold {fold}: train {fit_rows[0]}–{fit_rows[-1]}, " f"validate {valid_rows[0]}–{valid_rows[-1]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Fold 1: train 0–87, validate 88–119 Fold 2: train 0–119, validate 120–151 Fold 3: train 0–151, validate 152–183 ``` ::: ::: The final eight-day test period is excluded from every fold. ## How will we compare forecasts? **Mean absolute error (MAE)** is the average absolute prediction error, measured in **rentals per three-hour interval**. - An MAE of 5 means predictions miss by **five rentals on average**. - **Lower is better.** Compare mean validation MAE over the same three folds. - Start with simple forecasts before fitting more complex models. ## Simple forecasting baselines {.smaller} - **Persistence:** repeat the previous interval's count (`shift(1)`). - **Seasonal naive:** repeat the same interval yesterday (`shift(8)`). ::: {#c9865941 .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Previous interval 13.041667 Same interval yesterday 7.677083 Name: Validation MAE, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: These are successive one-step forecasts: completed counts become available between predictions. ## Reading the model comparisons {.smaller} - **Mean validation MAE:** averaged over all three temporal folds. - **Plots:** the same final fold for every model, showing the last training week and four validation days. - **Preprocessing:** fitted only on each fold's training rows, using pipelines. - **Final test:** reserved until we have selected a model. Training fit shows what a model can represent; validation error shows what carries forward. # Feature engineering for time series ## From timestamps to useful features - In this toy data, we just have a single feature: the date time feature. - Note that ML models do not have a built-in concept of time. We have to give it to them. - Start with a numeric timestamp, then add **calendar patterns**, **interactions**, and **recent observations**. ## POSIX time feature {.smaller} A simple numeric encoding is **seconds since the Unix epoch**, January 1, 1970, 00:00 UTC. Will a random forest learn repeating demand from one increasing number? ::: {#d75dd685 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} calendar[["elapsed_seconds"]].head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

This is exactly what happens with POSIX time encoded as a single numeric feature! ## Seasonality **Seasonality** refers to a **repeating pattern** that occurs at regular, predictable intervals. - **Example 1:** Bike rentals tend to peak at the same hours each day (daily seasonality). - **Example 2:** Retail sales consistently spike before the December holidays (annual seasonality). - Recognizing seasonality helps a model **anticipate recurring patterns** rather than mistake them for noise. - We can capture seasonality by adding features such as: `rush_hour`, `is_weekend`, and `is_holiday` ## Extracting date and time information - Note that our index is of this special type: [`DateTimeIndex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DatetimeIndex.html). We can extract all kinds of interesting information from it. ::: {#dd2312a6 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(citibike.index[0]) print(citibike.index[0].month_name()) print(citibike.index[0].dayofweek) print(citibike.index[0].hour) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2015-08-01 00:00:00 August 5 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Hour of day Hour-of-day values recur in future intervals, allowing a model to reuse daily patterns. ::: {#41e0df83 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} calendar[["hour"]].head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

Lag features describe **what happened recently**. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {#bae6f096 .cell execution_count=25} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}

Do not use this test result to choose another model. # Forecasting further into the future ## What changes when we forecast further ahead? - At **00:00 on September 1**, suppose we need predictions for the next five three-hour periods, through **12:00–15:00**. - The count for **21:00–00:00** is known. - Counts for periods starting at **00:00, 03:00, 06:00, and 09:00** are not yet known. **How can we build lag features for later predictions without those actual counts?** ## Approach 1: Iterative forecasting {.smaller} Train one model that predicts 3 hours ahead. At prediction time, move forward step by step, using your own predictions as future lag inputs. **Example:** - Predict rentals at 00:00 on 2015-09-01. - Use that prediction as the lag to predict rentals at 03:00. - Use both predictions to predict rentals at 06:00. - Continue until you reach 12:00. This method works, but errors accumulate as we step forward. The longer the horizon, the more uncertainty grows. ## Approach 2: Direct forecasting (multiple horizons) {.smaller} - Train separate models for each horizon: - Model 1 $\rightarrow$ predict 3 hours ahead - Model 2 $\rightarrow$ predict 6 hours ahead - Model 3 $\rightarrow$ predict 9 hours ahead All models use observations available at the **same forecast origin**. For each horizon, shift the target forward while keeping lag inputs in the known past. Future calendar features are also available. ## Optional: Multi-output forecasting {.slide-optional} - Train one model that predicts several future steps at once, e.g.: ```y = [rentals_in_3h, rentals_in_6h, rentals_in_9h, ...]``` - Some models share information across future steps; others fit outputs independently. - Note: Multi-output forecasting is powerful, but outside the scope of CPSC 330. # Modeling trends We have used calendar features for **repeating patterns**. What about **long-term change**? ## Trends {.smaller} Let's consider another time series dataset, [Retail Sales of Clothing and Clothing Accessory Stores dataset](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MRTSSM448USN). ::: {#5b4328b3 .cell execution_count=34} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-19-time-series_files/figure-revealjs/cell-35-output-1.png){width=666 height=357} ::: ::: It looks like there's a clear trend; retail sales gradually increase over time. A **trend** is a long-term upward or downward movement in a time series. Question: How might we encode this trend information so our models can use it? ## Days since feature {.smaller} Encode long-term change as **elapsed time from a fixed reference date**. ::: {#d1baf60c .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} first_day_retail = retail_df["date"].min() retail_with_time = retail_df.assign( Days_since=(retail_df["date"] - first_day_retail).dt.days ) retail_with_time.head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=35} ```{=html}
date sales Days_since
0 1992-01-01 6938 0
1 1992-02-01 7524 31
2 1992-03-01 8475 60
3 1992-04-01 9401 91
4 1992-05-01 9558 121
5 1992-06-01 9182 152
``` ::: ::: A linear model can learn a slope for this feature. A random forest still cannot extrapolate a trend beyond its training range. # Optional: Types of time series ## Univariate time series: Bike rentals {.slide-optional .smaller} A **univariate time series** tracks *one* variable over time. Here, we only measure the number of bike rentals at each timestamp. | starttime | rentals | |----------------------|---------| | 2015-08-26 12:00:00 | 30 | | 2015-08-12 09:00:00 | 10 | | 2015-08-19 03:00:00 | 2 | | 2015-08-07 12:00:00 | 22 | | 2015-08-03 09:00:00 | 9 | ## Multivariate time series {.slide-optional .smaller} A **multivariate time series** records several variables at each timestamp. Here, we track bike rentals along with weather and local traffic conditions. | datetime | rentals | temp_C | humidity | wind_kmh | traffic_level | |---------------------|---------|--------|----------|----------|----------------| | 2015-08-01 09:00 | 12 | 18 | 65 | 10 | 2 | | 2015-08-01 12:00 | 28 | 22 | 55 | 8 | 3 | | 2015-08-01 15:00 | 35 | 24 | 50 | 12 | 4 | | 2015-08-01 18:00 | 30 | 21 | 60 | 20 | 3 | | 2015-08-02 09:00 | 10 | 17 | 70 | 15 | 1 | ## Hierarchical time series {.slide-optional .smaller} Related time series form an aggregation hierarchy: store sales add up to city sales, and city sales add up to company sales. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} | city | store_id | date | bike_sales | |-----------|----------|-------------|------------| | Vancouver | S1 | 2024-01-01 | 12 | | Vancouver | S1 | 2024-01-02 | 15 | | Vancouver | S2 | 2024-01-01 | 9 | | Vancouver | S2 | 2024-01-02 | 11 | | Victoria | M1 | 2024-01-01 | 7 | | Victoria | M1 | 2024-01-02 | 8 | | Victoria | M2 | 2024-01-01 | 14 | | Victoria | M2 | 2024-01-02 | 13 | ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ``` Company ├── Vancouver │ ├── S1 time series │ └── S2 time series └── Victoria ├── M1 time series └── M2 time series ``` ::: :::: # Check out the [demo](https://ubc-cs.github.io/cpsc330-book/book/chapter-19-time-series-demo.html) ## Back to today's big questions {.slide-summary .smaller} 1. **What changes with time order?** Recent observations, repeating patterns (**seasonality**), and long-term **trends** can inform predictions. 2. **How do we evaluate forecasts?** Compare baselines and models using temporal validation MAE; fit preprocessing within folds, then evaluate the selected model once on the final test. 3. **Which features help?** Calendar, interaction, lag, and elapsed-time features; their encoding must suit the model. Trees cannot extrapolate trends. 4. **How do we forecast further ahead?** Use predictions as future lag inputs (**iterative**) or train a model for each horizon (**direct**). **Baseline → temporal validation → model selection → one final test.**
